### Alashan vs Ordos vs Mongolian Cashmere Goats: What's the Real Difference?

*Published 2026-07-24*

Not all cashmere goats are the same. Alashan, Ordos, and Mongolian goats produce measurably different fiber — micron, length, color, down content. A 23-year Ordos factory's honest comparison.

# Alashan vs Ordos vs Mongolian Cashmere Goats: What's the Real Difference?

The label says "100% cashmere" but the goat behind that fiber matters. A 14.5μm Grade A cashmere from an Alashan goat is not the same as a 15.5μm Grade B from a lowland Mongolian goat. The difference shows up in micron, length, color, and how the finished garment ages.

Below is an honest comparison of the three main Inner Asian cashmere goat populations — based on 23 years of buying raw fiber from herders across these regions.

## The 3 main cashmere goat populations

**Alashan goats** (阿拉善白绒山羊)
- **Region:** Alashan League, western Inner Mongolia (~39°N, 105°E)
- **Population:** ~1.5 million head (smallest of the three)
- **Climate:** Extreme continental desert — 40°C summers, -25°C winters, <100mm rainfall
- **Fiber color:** Mostly white (the most valuable for dyeing)
- **Famous for:** The finest micron in the world — true Grade A cashmere is 90%+ from Alashan

**Ordos goats** (阿尔巴斯白绒山羊, Arbas white cashmere goat)
- **Region:** Ordos City, southern Inner Mongolia (~39°N, 109°E)
- **Population:** ~3 million head
- **Climate:** High plateau (1,300m altitude), semi-arid grassland
- **Fiber color:** White, brown, gray mix
- **Famous for:** The "Arbas goat" is China's national geographic indication product — protected designation since 2001

**Mongolian goats** (蒙古白绒山羊, Mongolian white cashmere goat)
- **Region:** All across Mongolia (Outer Mongolia, not Inner Mongolia)
- **Population:** ~30 million head (largest population)
- **Climate:** High plateau (1,500m+), extreme continental — 35°C summers, -40°C winters
- **Fiber color:** Mostly white, some brown/gray
- **Famous for:** Largest cashmere-producing country by volume (~40% of global supply)

## Measurable fiber differences

| Property | Alashan | Ordos | Mongolian |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Avg. micron (μm)** | 14.0-15.5 | 14.5-16.0 | 15.0-16.5 |
| **Avg. fiber length (mm)** | 36-42 | 32-38 | 32-40 |
| **Down content (%)** | 95-98 | 90-95 | 85-92 |
| **Guard hair ratio** | 2-5% | 5-10% | 8-15% |
| **Natural color (most common)** | White | White/Brown/Gray | White/Brown/Gray |
| **Yields per goat (g/yr)** | 250-350 | 200-300 | 150-250 |
| **Annual production (tons)** | ~3,500 | ~7,000 | ~9,000 |

Source: Industry estimates based on 2020-2024 sourcing data, cross-referenced with the Inner Mongolia Bureau of Animal Husbandry.

## What each goat is best for

**Alashan Grade A** — For luxury knitwear and ultra-fine scarves where hand feel is the dominant purchase factor. 14.5μm fiber with 38mm length makes yarn that's nearly weightless. Price premium of 30-50% over equivalent-grade Ordos.

**Ordos Grade A/B** — The best balance of quality and price. Ordos Arbas goats produce slightly longer fiber than Alashan (good for yarn spinning efficiency) at a 15-20% lower price. Most mid-market and premium DTC brands use Ordos fiber.

**Mongolian Grade B/C** — The workhorse of the cashmere industry. Mongolian fiber is widely available at scale, with consistent quality. Best for sweaters at USD 80-200 retail, blends, and private label brands prioritizing margin.

## Honest disclosures

**"Alashan" doesn't always mean true Alashan fiber.** Some yarn suppliers blend Alashan fiber with other regions and still call it "Alashan cashmere". A truly 100% Alashan yarn supplier will show you the herder cooperative agreement, GPS coordinates, and batch traceability. We work with two certified Alashan cooperatives.

**"Mongolian cashmere" sometimes means Chinese fiber shipped through Mongolia.** The reverse is also true. True geographic origin requires documentation from the herder cooperative, not just the country of export.

**"Grade A" is not standardized.** As we covered in the [Cashmere Grades](/en/cashmere-grades) guide, the A/B/C grading system is industry convention, not a regulated standard. Always ask for actual micron readings, not just verbal claims.

## How we source

Our dehaired cashmere comes from a mix of:
- **40% Alashan Grade A** (for our luxury scarf and premium sweater lines)
- **45% Ordos Arbas Grade A/B** (for our standard sweater and yarn offerings)
- **15% Mongolian Grade B** (for blending and entry-level lines)

Every batch ships with a Certificate of Origin listing the herder cooperative and approximate GPS coordinates of the source pasture. This isn't required by law — we do it because the fiber origin is the only thing that actually distinguishes premium cashmere from commodity cashmere.

## Why this matters for your brand

If you're a private label brand sourcing cashmere, the **fiber origin** is the single biggest quality signal you can pass to your end customer. Most DTC brands (Naadam, Quince, Everlane) market "Mongolian cashmere" or "Inner Mongolian cashmere" because that's where most volume comes from. Few can credibly claim "Alashan Grade A" or "Arbas protected designation".

If you have a 200-piece private label order, mixing in 30-50% Alashan fiber gives you a real differentiation story — and a hand feel your customers will actually feel. We can blend to your specification.

### Why Cashmere Costs USD 8-50 per Piece: A Factory's True Cost Breakdown

*Published 2026-07-24*

A transparent cost breakdown of a finished cashmere sweater from raw fiber to FOB Tianjin — material, labor, overhead, margin. What every B2B buyer should know before negotiating.

# Why Cashmere Costs USD 8-50 per Piece: A Factory's True Cost Breakdown

"Why does cashmere cost so much?" is the most common question we get from new B2B buyers. The short answer: raw cashmere fiber alone costs USD 50-120 per kg, and a single sweater uses 300-500g of it. But the full picture involves more than just fiber.

Below is a **transparent cost breakdown** of a finished Grade A 14.5μm cashmere sweater, FOB Tianjin, for a 500-piece private label order. We've stripped out our margin so you can see what the actual cost structure looks like.

## The sweater we're costing

- **Product:** Crew-neck pullover, 14-gauge, 12 gg flat knit
- **Yarn:** 2/48 Nm worsted, 100% Grade A dehaired cashmere (14.5μm, 38mm)
- **Weight:** 380g per piece (medium-weight, men's M)
- **Order:** 500 pieces, 1 color (camel)
- **Incoterms:** FOB Tianjin

## Cost line items

| # | Line item | USD per piece | % of total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Raw cashmere fiber (380g @ USD 75/kg, Grade A) | $28.50 | 51% |
| 2 | Yarn spinning (worsted, 2/48 Nm, 1kg fiber = 0.85kg yarn) | $4.50 | 8% |
| 3 | Knitting (STOLL machine, 18 minutes per piece, 1 operator) | $3.20 | 6% |
| 4 | Linking (seaming by hand, 25 minutes per piece) | $4.00 | 7% |
| 5 | Washing + softening (wet process, 30 min) | $1.80 | 3% |
| 6 | Ironing + final pressing (10 min) | $0.90 | 2% |
| 7 | Woven main label + care label + paper hangtag | $0.40 | 1% |
| 8 | Polybag + inner box + outer carton (5 pcs/ctn) | $0.70 | 1% |
| 9 | QC inspection (AQL 2.5 sampling, 30 min) | $0.50 | 1% |
| 10 | Factory overhead (utilities, rent, depreciation) | $3.50 | 6% |
| 11 | Labor (wages, benefits, social insurance) | $5.00 | 9% |
| 12 | Export packaging + documentation | $0.80 | 1% |
| 13 | **Subtotal (production cost)** | **$53.80** | **96%** |
| 14 | Factory margin (15%) | $8.07 | 14% |
| 15 | **FOB Tianjin price** | **$61.87** | **110%** |

So a Grade A men's cashmere sweater costs about **USD 62 FOB Tianjin** for a 500-piece order. The breakdown shows why: **raw fiber alone is 51% of the cost**. This is why "cheap cashmere" is almost always a red flag — either the fiber is lower grade (15.5-19μm), or it's blended with wool or recycled fiber.

## What changes the price by 30-50%?

The biggest cost variables, in order of impact:

**1. Fiber grade (most impactful)**
- Grade A (14-15.5μm): USD 75-120/kg raw
- Grade B (15.5-16.5μm): USD 50-75/kg raw
- Grade C (16.5-19μm): USD 30-50/kg raw

A Grade B sweater of the same design: ~USD 42 FOB. A Grade C: ~USD 28 FOB.

**2. Order quantity (volume discount)**
- 100 pieces: ~USD 75 FOB (set-up costs amortized)
- 500 pieces: ~USD 62 FOB
- 2,000+ pieces: ~USD 52 FOB

The set-up costs (yarn lot minimum, machine programming, label production) are fixed regardless of order size.

**3. Gauge (yarn count)**
- 7gg chunky: heavier (500g+), more fiber per piece → ~USD 75 FOB
- 12gg standard: 380g → ~USD 62 FOB
- 16gg fine: 280g → ~USD 48 FOB

Finer gauge = less fiber = lower cost, but slower machine speed (more expensive knitting time per piece).

**4. Custom vs. stock design**
- Stock design (no programming): no extra cost
- Custom design (programming, sampling): +USD 200-500 setup, spread across the order

For first-time private label brands, starting with a stock design saves 1-2 weeks of sampling time and ~USD 500 in set-up.

## What's NOT in this price

The USD 62 FOB Tianjin price above is the **factory gate price**. It does NOT include:
- **Ocean freight** (USD 2-4 per piece for FCL to EU/US, depending on volume)
- **Customs duties** (US: 0% for cashmere under HTS 6110; EU: 12% VAT + 4% duty)
- **Import handling** (USD 0.50-1.50 per piece for customs broker + drayage)
- **Marketing / brand investment** (varies wildly)
- **Retail markup** (typically 2.5-4x wholesale for DTC brands)

So a USD 62 FOB cashmere sweater lands at the US port for about **USD 67-70 all-in**. A DTC brand selling at USD 280 retail has a 76% gross margin at this landed cost — before marketing, photography, customer service, returns.

## Why "USD 8 cashmere" is not a real product

You'll see sweaters marketed as "cashmere" at USD 8-15 on Amazon, fast-fashion sites, and discount platforms. These are almost always:
- **Recycled cashmere** (shoddy pulled from old garments, re-spun — short fibers, pills within 2 wears)
- **Cashmere/wool blend** (sometimes 70% wool, 30% cashmere — the label just says "cashmere blend")
- **Grade C cashmere** (16.5-19μm — coarser, scratchier, often blended with 20-30% viscose to soften the hand feel)
- **Mislabeled** (no actual cashmere content; Chinese or Turkish acrylic marketed as "cashmere-like")

If the price seems too good to be true, it isn't cashmere. Use the cost breakdown above as a sanity check: any "cashmere sweater" priced below USD 25 FOB equivalent is, at best, 30% cashmere with the rest being wool or synthetic.

## How to negotiate price without losing quality

The right way to bring the cost down is **not** to push the factory on margin (which compresses their ability to maintain quality), but to:
1. **Increase order quantity** (500 → 2,000+ pieces saves ~15%)
2. **Choose a more efficient gauge** (12gg → 14gg saves ~10% on fiber)
3. **Use Grade B instead of Grade A** (saves ~30% on fiber, hand feel still excellent)
4. **Combine SKUs in one production run** (amortizes set-up across more pieces)
5. **Book production 60+ days in advance** (better yarn pricing, factory capacity discounts)

A factory that drops price by 30% in negotiation is signaling they'll cut corners on fiber, labor, or quality control. The honest factory will explain the trade-offs and let you choose.

### How to Wash, Dry, and Store Cashmere: A Factory's Honest Care Guide

*Published 2026-07-24*

Hand wash, machine wash, dry clean — what's actually safe for cashmere? How to fix pilling, remove stains, and store cashmere so it lasts 10+ years. A practical care guide from a 23-year cashmere manufacturer.

# How to Wash, Dry, and Store Cashmere: A Factory's Honest Care Guide

Cashmere is a natural fiber. Treat it well and it lasts 10+ years. Treat it poorly and it pills, shrinks, or loses shape in 6 months. After 23 years of watching how customers care for their cashmere, here's the honest guide.

## The 3 ways to wash cashmere (ranked by safety)

**1. Hand wash (safest)** — Always works. Use cool water (30°C max) and a pH-neutral wool wash (we like Eucalan or Soak, no rinsing required). Submerge for 15-20 minutes. Gently press (don't wring) the water out. Roll in a clean towel to remove excess moisture. Lay flat to dry on a fresh towel, reshaping gently.

**2. Machine wash (acceptable, with conditions)** — Most modern washing machines have a "wool" or "delicates" cycle that mimics hand washing. Use:
- Cool water (cold setting, 30°C max)
- Wool-safe detergent (NOT regular detergent, NOT fabric softener)
- Mesh laundry bag (essential — prevents snagging and agitation damage)
- Lowest spin speed (or no spin)
- Wash similar colors together (camel + ivory are fine; white + dark = trouble)

**NEVER** use hot water, regular detergent, or high spin. Hot water + agitation = felted cashmere (irreversible shrinkage).

**3. Dry cleaning (works but with caveats)** — Most dry cleaners use perchloroethylene (perc) which doesn't damage cashmere but isn't great for the environment. Some "green" cleaners use CO2 or water-based methods. If you dry clean, request "gentle cycle" and "low heat". Avoid dry cleaning more than 2-3 times per year — the solvents strip natural oils from the fiber over time.

Our honest recommendation: **hand wash if you have 20 minutes, machine wash on wool cycle if you're in a hurry, dry clean only for stubborn stains.**

## Drying cashmere (this is where most people ruin their sweaters)

**THE BIGGEST MISTAKE:** Hanging a wet cashmere sweater to dry. The water weight stretches the fiber, leaving the shoulders deformed and the body elongated — permanently.

**Correct method:**
1. After washing, gently press water out (don't wring)
2. Roll in a clean dry towel, press to absorb (repeat with second dry towel if very wet)
3. Lay flat on a fresh dry towel, reshape to original dimensions
4. Keep away from direct sunlight and direct heat (radiators, hair dryers)
5. Flip after 8-12 hours; should be dry in 24-36 hours

Drying takes patience. **Never** put cashmere in a dryer (even on low heat). Even 10 minutes in a tumble dryer can cause irreversible shrinkage and felting.

## Pilling: what causes it, how to fix it

Pilling (those tiny fiber balls on the surface) is **not a quality defect** — it's a natural response to friction. New cashmere sweaters pill more in the first 3-4 wears as loose fibers come to the surface. After the initial pilling phase, good cashmere pills minimally for years.

**Where pilling happens most:**
- Underarm area (most friction from arm movement)
- Inner elbow (bending friction)
- Side torso (bag/strap friction)
- Cuffs (desk/friction contact)

**How to remove pills safely:**
- **Cashmere comb** (best tool) — fine-toothed comb specifically designed for knitwear. Lay the sweater flat, comb gently in one direction.
- **Fabric shaver** (also good) — electric de-piller like the Philips Fabric Shaver or Conair Fabric Defuzzer. Use on low setting, light pressure. Don't go over the same spot repeatedly.
- **Avoid:** Regular razors (cuts the fiber), tape (pulls fibers), scissors (cuts too much).

**How to prevent pilling long-term:**
- Wash inside out (reduces surface friction)
- Don't wear the same cashmere 2 days in a row (fiber needs 24 hours to recover)
- Store folded, not hung (hanging stretches shoulders)
- Use a cashmere wash (preserves natural oils)

A cashmere sweater that pills heavily in year 1 is a quality red flag. But pilling lightly in months 1-3, then stabilizing, is normal — even for Grade A.

## Stain removal (specific stain types)

**Oil-based stains** (makeup, salad dressing, butter): Sprinkle cornstarch or baby powder on the stain immediately. Let sit 30 minutes to absorb. Then hand wash with wool detergent. Repeat if needed. Do NOT use hot water first — sets the stain.

**Water-based stains** (coffee, wine, juice): Blot (don't rub) with cold water from the inside of the fabric. Apply a tiny amount of wool detergent, work in gently. Rinse. Repeat if needed.

**Deodorant marks:** Mix white vinegar and water 50/50. Dab on the mark, let sit 10 minutes, then wash normally.

**Moth holes:** Prevention is everything — see storage below. If you find a hole, take it to a tailor for repair. A skilled tailor can reweave small holes invisibly.

## Storage (off-season + daily)

**Daily storage:** Fold, don't hang. Hanging stretches shoulders permanently. Use a shelf or drawer with room for the sweater to "breathe" — don't cram it in.

**Off-season storage** (3+ months not worn):
1. Wash before storing (body oils and food residue attract moths)
2. Completely dry (moisture + closed storage = mildew)
3. Use **cedar blocks, lavender sachets, or moth balls** (naphthalene) — DO NOT use plastic garment bags for long-term storage; cashmere needs to breathe
4. Store in a **cotton storage bag** (not plastic) in a cool, dry place
5. Check every 2-3 months for moth activity

**Moth prevention is critical.** Clothes moths (Tineola bisselliella) lay eggs in natural fibers — including cashmere. A single moth can lay 100+ eggs, and the larvae eat cashmere fiber. If you see one moth, check ALL your cashmere immediately.

## What we tell our B2B customers to include with each sale

If you're a private label cashmere brand, the care guide is the single most important insert to include with each garment. It directly determines:
- **Customer satisfaction** (pilling complaints drop 80% when customers understand the first-3-wear pilling phase)
- **Repeat purchase rate** (customers who know how to care for cashmere buy again 2-3x more often)
- **Returns** (proper care prevents "this cashmere is ruined" returns)

Most brands skip the care insert. The ones that include it build lifetime customers.

## When to retire a cashmere sweater

With proper care, a Grade A cashmere sweater should last 8-15 years. Signs it's time to retire:
- **Holes that can't be invisibly repaired** (large, in visible spots)
- **Permanent felting** (the fiber has matted together — usually from a hot wash incident)
- **Major pilling that doesn't respond to combing** (usually means the fiber is wearing through)

Most "cashmere ruined" stories involve one of three things: hot water wash, tumble dryer, or stored with body oils attracting moths. Avoid those three and your cashmere will outlive most of your wardrobe.

## Frequently asked questions about washing and caring for cashmere
Retail customers, brand owners, and care-instruction writers ask the same questions about keeping cashmere garments in good condition. These quick answers cover the most common care mistakes and the recovery actions for each. To request care-instruction cards for your private-label cashmere line, see our [customization options](/en/contact).

### Can I machine-wash cashmere?
It depends on the cashmere garment and the washing machine. Modern cashmere garments with machine-knit construction (12gg+, 2-ply worsted) can typically be machine-washed on a delicate/wool cycle at 30°C (86°F) with a pH-neutral wool detergent, in a mesh laundry bag, with the spin cycle disabled or set to 400 RPM max. Hand-knit or loosely-knitted cashmere (7gg chunky, single-ply) should be hand-washed only. The safest approach for any cashmere garment: hand-wash in cool water (30°C max) with a wool detergent, gently press (do not wring), and lay flat to dry on a clean towel. Never put cashmere in a hot wash or hot dryer — heat causes the fiber to shrink irreversibly, and agitation causes pilling.

### How do I remove pilling from a cashmere sweater?
Cashmere pilling is normal — it appears under the arms, on the sides, and where the garment rubs against itself or outerwear. To remove pilling safely: use a cashmere comb or a fabric shaver (electric sweater shaver) on a flat, dry garment. Hold the fabric taut and run the comb or shaver gently over the pilled area; do not press hard. Avoid using regular razors ( can cut the fiber) and avoid pulling pills off by hand (distorts the knit structure). Pilling typically subsides after 3–5 wear cycles as loose fiber ends work their way out of the yarn structure. Premium cashmere (14.0–15.5μm, 36+mm staple length) pills significantly less than entry-grade cashmere (16.5–19.0μm, 24–30mm staple length).

### How should I store cashmere during summer?
Cashmere garments should be stored during the off-season as follows: clean the garment thoroughly before storing (body oils and food residue attract moths), fold (do not hang — hanging distorts shoulder shape), wrap in acid-free tissue paper or store in a breathable cotton storage bag, place in a cool, dry location (15–22°C, 45–55% humidity), and add a natural moth repellent (cedar blocks, lavender sachets, or rosemary). Avoid: plastic bags (trap moisture and cause yellowing), cardboard boxes (acidic, weakens fiber over time), and mothballs (chemical residue damages fiber). Inspect stored cashmere monthly — moth damage usually appears as small holes in concealed areas (under collars, inside folds). For long-term storage (more than 6 months), consider professional cleaning and storage at a specialist.

### Why does cashmere get holes even with proper care?
Cashmere develops small holes primarily from moth larvae (the most common cause), fabric damage from friction (seat belt, rough table edges, backpack straps), or fiber degradation from improper cleaning (chlorine bleach, hot water, harsh detergents). Moth larvae prefer natural fibers (cashmere, wool, silk) and feed on body oil residue; clean garments in breathable storage are less attractive to moths. To prevent holes: wash or dry-clean before storage, use moth repellents, rotate garments in your wardrobe (moths prefer undisturbed items), and trim any loose threads immediately (pulled threads become holes). Small holes can be invisibly mended by a specialist tailor or alteration service; do not attempt home repair with sewing — cashmere knit structure is complex and home repairs usually make holes worse.

### Can I dry-clean cashmere?
Yes — dry-cleaning is safe for cashmere garments and is often the recommended care method for tailored cashmere (blazers, structured knitwear, lined garments). Use a dry cleaner experienced with cashmere and request "clean fresh solvent only, no perc" if possible. Dry-cleaning after every 4–5 wears is reasonable for frequently-worn cashmere blazers and coats; less frequent dry-cleaning is fine for casual cashmere pullovers. Avoid "wet cleaning" at the dry cleaner unless they specifically handle cashmere — some wet-cleaning processes use agitation that causes shrinkage. Always check the care label first: some hand-knit cashmere is labeled "dry clean only," while machine-knit cashmere can typically be hand-washed at home with similar results at lower cost.

### What is the best way to de-wrinkle cashmere?
To de-wrinkle cashmere safely: steam is the preferred method — hang the garment in a steamy bathroom for 10–15 minutes, or use a handheld steamer held 10+ cm from the fabric (do not press the steamer directly onto the cashmere). Avoid: ironing directly on cashmere (heat and pressure crush the fiber); ironing on high heat; tumble drying. For deeper wrinkles, a low-temperature iron with a pressing cloth (cotton or linen) between the iron and the cashmere works — set iron to "wool" or 110°C max, press gently, do not slide the iron. After de-wrinkling, lay the garment flat to cool and dry before hanging or wearing. If the cashmere develops a permanent crease (after long-term improper folding), wash and lay flat to reshape; deep-set creases may require professional pressing.

### Dehaired Cashmere Tops: The Complete B2B Buyer's Guide to Combed Cashmere from Ordos

*Published 2026-07-08*

Not all dehaired cashmere is equal. Combed top quality varies by micron uniformity, fiber alignment, and residual guard hair. A buyer's guide to selecting the right dehaired cashmere for your spinning process.

# Dehaired Cashmere Tops: The Complete B2B Buyer's Guide

**Dehaired cashmere** is the post-processed fiber that spinners actually work with. It comes from combing out guard hair and impurities from raw (greasy) cashmere. The quality of this step determines whether your finished yarn is luxury-grade or full of pills after three wears.

This guide covers what separates premium dehaired cashmere from commodity fiber.

## What "dehaired" actually means

Raw cashmere combed from goats is called **greasy cashmere** — a tangled mass of fine underdown (the valuable part), thick guard hair (useless for spinning), lanolin, dirt, and vegetable matter.

**Dehairing** is the mechanical process of separating the fine underdown from the guard hair. The result is a clean, aligned **cashmere top** (also called a combed top or roving) that can be drawn into yarn.

The process is purely mechanical — modern dehaiiring lines use no chemicals, no water, no dye. Italian-made Capstan and similar equipment have been the industry standard for 30+ years.

## The 4 grades of dehaired cashmere

After dehairing, fiber is sorted by **micron count** (fiber diameter, measured in micrometers):

| Grade | Micron | Use case | Price (USD/kg) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Superfine white** | 14.5-15.5μm | Luxury knitwear, fine-gauge scarves | $120-160 |
| **Standard white** | 15.0-16.0μm | Mid-luxury knitwear, premium blending | $90-115 |
| **Brown (qing)** | 15.5-16.5μm | Heathered yarns, workwear | $80-100 |
| **Purple (zi)** | 16.0-17.5μm | Felted products, low-end blends | $65-85 |

For B2B buyers sourcing for luxury or mid-luxury brands, **Superfine white** and **Standard white** are 90% of the market.

## 5 quality indicators in dehaired cashmere

A premium dehaired cashmere top has the following characteristics. Test any sample for these before committing to a bulk order.

### 1. **Fiber parallel alignment**

A properly combed top has fibers running roughly parallel along its length. Hold a small tuft up to the light — you should see a uniform sheen without visible "tangles" or "clumps."

A poorly dehaired top has fibers in random orientations, making it harder to spin and resulting in weaker, hairier yarn.

### 2. **Residual guard hair content**

Under 40x magnification (a $30 USB microscope works), count guard hair fibers in a 1g sample. Premium dehaired cashmere should have **< 1% guard hair by count**. Anything above 3% suggests incomplete dehairing.

Guard hair in finished yarn shows up as "frizzies" — thick, straight fibers that don't take dye the same as cashmere and create a coarse, itchy hand feel.

### 3. **Micron uniformity (CV%)**

Beyond the mean micron count, look at the **coefficient of variation** (CV%) — the standard deviation divided by the mean. A premium dehaired top has **CV < 20%**. Anything above 25% means the fiber is mixed (different goats, different ages, or blended batches).

A high CV shows up in your yarn as inconsistent dyeing and uneven texture — some fibers absorb dye differently, creating a "heathered" look you didn't intend.

### 4. **Moisture content**

Premium dehaired cashmere should have **< 12% moisture content** (regain). Above 15% means:
- The fiber wasn't properly dried
- You're paying for water weight, not fiber
- Risk of mold in storage

A simple moisture meter ($100-200) gives instant readings. Any supplier refusing to provide moisture data is hiding something.

### 5. **Color uniformity within bale**

Real "white" cashmere has subtle color variation — different goats, different body parts, different ages contribute. Perfectly uniform bright-white fiber has been **bleached**, which damages the cuticle and shortens fiber life.

Take 5-10 random samples from different parts of a bale. Subtle variation (ivory to light gray) is normal. Identical bright white across all samples suggests processing.

## Combed top vs. open top: which to choose?

Dehaired cashmere comes in two forms:

- **Combed top** (roving): Fibers are parallel-aligned into a continuous rope. Used for **worsted spinning** (smooth, strong yarn for machine knitting and weaving).
- **Open top** (sliver): Fibers are randomized. Used for **woolen spinning** (soft, lofty yarn for hand knitting and chunky sweaters).

For machine knitting 12+ gauge, you want combed top. For hand knitting or 5-7 gauge chunky, open top is fine.

**Most Ordos factories offer both**, but premium mills (like ours) specialize in combed top because luxury knitwear uses fine machine gauges.

## Lead time and MOQ for dehaired cashmere

- **MOQ**: 100kg per grade/color
- **Stock lead time**: 7-10 days (white cashmere usually in stock)
- **Custom lead time**: 20-25 days (custom micron sorting or custom dehairing)
- **Annual capacity**: Major Ordos mills dehair 800-1,200+ tons per year
- **Pricing**: Quoted FOB Tianjin/Shanghai; CIF your port available; DDP for EU/US

For new buyers, we recommend a **200-500kg trial order** before committing to a full-season volume. This lets you test the fiber in your own spinning process and validate the quality.

## Working with a dehaired cashmere supplier

When evaluating a new dehaired cashmere supplier, ask these 5 questions:

1. **"What's your annual dehaiiring capacity?"** — A real dehaiiring facility should dehair 500+ tons per year. Less than that and they're likely a small operation with limited stock.
2. **"Do you have Italian dehaiiring lines?"** — Capstan, Marzoli, or similar. Chinese-made dehaiiring lines exist but quality is generally lower.
3. **"Can I visit and see the dehaiiring in operation?"** — A reputable facility hosts dozens of buyer audits per year.
4. **"Do you provide per-bale OFDA data?"** — Non-negotiable for premium cashmere.
5. **"What's your minimum micron guarantee for 'premium white'?"** — If they say 15.5μm or higher, look elsewhere. Real premium white is 14.5-15.5μm.

At DONGXIAO, all our dehaired white cashmere is 14.5-15.5μm with CV < 20%, and ships with full OFDA + length distribution data per bale.

### Direct Cashmere Mill, No Middleman: How to Buy from the Source and Skip the Trading Company Markup

*Published 2026-07-08*

Trading companies add 30-40% to cashmere prices. For B2B buyers ordering 500kg+, sourcing direct from the mill cuts out the middleman — but requires different logistics.

# Direct Cashmere Mill, No Middleman: A B2B Guide

The cashmere industry has a **30-40% middleman tax**. Most B2B buyers in Europe and North America don't buy directly from a Chinese cashmere factory — they buy from a **trading company** in Hong Kong, Istanbul, or Milan that adds 30-40% margin and provides local language support.

For B2B buyers ordering 500kg+ per shipment, **sourcing direct from the mill** cuts out the middleman and saves 25-35% on per-unit cost.

But direct sourcing has trade-offs. This guide covers when it makes sense, and how to do it right.

## The 3 middleman models in cashmere

### Model 1: Hong Kong trading company

Most common for B2B exports to EU/US. Trading companies based in HK:
- **Add 30-40% margin** to factory price
- **Provide**: English/European language support, smaller MOQ flexibility, inventory financing, logistics management
- **Best for**: Buyers under 200kg per shipment, or who value convenience over cost

### Model 2: Italian/Scottish commission agent

Common for ultra-luxury buyers. Local agents who:
- **Add 20-30% commission** but also provide local QC and storage
- **Specialize in**: Specific factories (e.g., they represent only 2-3 mills)
- **Best for**: Buyers who want a "local partner" in the cashmere trade

### Model 3: Turkish processor

For buyers wanting finished products, Turkish factories often buy Chinese yarn, knit/finish locally, then re-export. They add 50-80% margin (yarn + labor + overhead) but offer faster delivery to EU/US.

**Best for**: Buyers who want "Made in Turkey" label for tariff or marketing reasons

## When direct sourcing makes sense

Direct mill sourcing pays off when:

1. **Order volume is 500kg+ per shipment** — fixed costs (travel, communication, documentation) get spread over more units
2. **You have a logistics partner** — freight forwarder, customs broker, or warehouse in destination country
3. **You can communicate in English** (most Chinese factories have English-speaking sales staff)
4. **You can pay 30% T/T deposit, 70% before shipment** (standard Chinese payment terms)
5. **You can accept 30-45 day production lead time** + 25-35 day shipping

If your order is under 200kg per shipment, or you can't accept these terms, a trading company is the right choice.

## Cost comparison: direct vs. middleman

Same product (premium white dehaired cashmere, FOB Tianjin):

| Sourcing model | Per-kg cost | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct from mill** | $90-105 | Fiber only, FOB Tianjin, you handle shipping |
| **HK trading company** | $120-145 | Fiber + HK warehousing + English support + LCL shipping to your port |
| **Italian agent** | $130-155 | Fiber + local QC + EU customs clearance + storage |

The "savings" from direct sourcing (25-35%) is real — but you take on:
- **Travel** to Ordos for audit and quality verification (1-2 trips per year, $2,000-5,000 each)
- **Communication overhead** — factory speaks English but you handle the time zone, holiday calendars, etc.
- **Logistics** — you arrange shipping, customs, warehousing

For a 1,000kg order:
- Direct: $90-105K fiber + ~$5K logistics = **$95-110K total**
- HK trader: $120-145K including shipping = **$120-145K total**
- **Savings: $25-35K**

The savings are real for serious B2B buyers. The question is whether you have the operational capacity to manage direct sourcing.

## The 4 steps to direct sourcing

### Step 1: Initial factory outreach

- **Search B2B platforms** (Alibaba, Made-in-China) for "OEKO-TEX cashmere factory" — most legitimate factories have certifications displayed
- **Visit trade shows** (Première Vision Paris, SpinExpo, Intertextile Shanghai) — meet factories face-to-face
- **Industry referrals** — ask other cashmere buyers for factory recommendations
- **Verify the factory is real**: do they own the production line? (most trading companies don't)

**Send your initial inquiry** with:
- Target fiber/yarn/garment type
- Quantity and frequency
- Target price range
- Certifications required
- Delivery destination

### Step 2: Factory audit (essential)

**Visit the factory in person** before placing any bulk order. In 1-2 days at the facility, you can verify:

- **Real production lines** (vs. a trading company that just has an office)
- **OFDA equipment** in-house (means they test, not just claim)
- **Bale tracking** from herder to customer
- **Storage conditions**
- **Workforce size and skill**

Bring a **cashmere expert** (or hire a local consultant, ~$500/day) for the first audit. After 2-3 audits, you'll know the factory well enough to skip the expert.

### Step 3: Trial order

Start with a **small trial order** (typically 200-500kg or 100-300 units for garments) to test:
- **Quality consistency** — does the bulk match the sample?
- **Communication speed** — how long does the factory take to respond?
- **Logistics** — can they ship on time?
- **Payment terms** — do they honor the agreed payment schedule?

A trial order also lets you test the **paperwork flow** — commercial invoice, packing list, certificate of origin, OEKO-TEX certificate, OFDA test report, etc.

### Step 4: Scale to standing orders

Once the trial is successful, move to a **standing order** or **rolling forecast** model. This gives you:
- **Better pricing** (typically 5-10% lower than one-off orders)
- **Priority production** during peak season (Aug-Nov)
- **Stable supply** when other buyers are scrambling

A typical standing order: 1,000-2,000kg per month, with 3-6 month rolling forecast.

## Payment and documentation for direct sourcing

Standard Chinese factory payment terms:

- **30% T/T deposit** on order confirmation
- **70% T/T balance** before shipment
- **L/C at sight** for new customers (more secure but $200-500 bank fees)
- **OA (open account)** for A-grade customers after 6-12 months of trading history

Standard documents the factory should provide:

- **Commercial invoice** (in English and your local language)
- **Packing list** (weight, dimensions, quantity)
- **Bill of lading** (for sea) or **airway bill** (for air)
- **Certificate of origin** (Form A, Form E, or Form F depending on your country)
- **OEKO-TEX certificate** (if applicable)
- **OFDA test report** (per bale, if requested)
- **Insurance certificate** (if you bought CIF insurance)

**Always use a freight forwarder** experienced in Chinese textile exports for the first 3-5 orders. They handle customs documentation, port handling, and shipping coordination for $200-500 per shipment.

## The 5 risks of direct sourcing (and how to manage them)

### Risk 1: Quality mismatch

Sample is great, bulk is mediocre.

**Mitigation**: Specify per-bale OFDA testing in your PO. Reject any bale that doesn't meet spec. Most reputable factories will accept returns on quality issues.

### Risk 2: Late delivery

Chinese factories often have capacity issues in Q3-Q4 (peak season). Delays of 2-4 weeks are common.

**Mitigation**: Build buffer stock. Order 3-4 weeks earlier than you think you need.

### Risk 3: Communication issues

Time zones, language nuances, holiday schedules (Chinese New Year, National Day).

**Mitigation**: Use email for written records. Schedule weekly calls. Be clear about expectations.

### Risk 4: Currency fluctuation

RMB-USD exchange rate can move 5-10% per year.

**Mitigation**: Use forward contracts for orders over $50K. Or pay in USD via L/C.

### Risk 5: IP protection

Sending designs to a Chinese factory carries inherent risk of copying.

**Mitigation**: Use NDAs. Start with non-core designs. Build trust over 2-3 years before sending your best work.

## Working with DONGXIAO directly

We work with a mix of:

### How to Verify Ordos Cashmere: 7 Tests Every B2B Buyer Should Run Before Signing a PO

*Published 2026-07-08*

Origin fraud, fiber blending, and micron inflation cost B2B buyers millions annually. A practical guide to verifying your Ordos cashmere supplier's claims with 7 lab and on-site tests.

# How to Verify Ordos Cashmere: 7 Tests Every B2B Buyer Should Run

Origin fraud in the cashmere trade is real. A 2023 industry survey estimated 25-35% of "Mongolian cashmere" sold in Western markets is either blended with non-Mongolian fiber, chemically treated, or both. For B2B buyers paying $100+ per kg for premium fiber, that adds up fast.

This guide covers the 7 tests that separate real Ordos cashmere from clever marketing — most cost under $200 and can be done before your first shipment.

## Test 1: OFDA micron scan (the gold standard)

The single most important cashmere test. **OFDA 2000** is a laser-scanning instrument that measures fiber diameter on 2,000+ fibers per sample, producing a mean and standard deviation.

**What to look for**:
- **Premium white cashmere**: 14.5-15.5μm mean, σ < 1.0μm
- **Standard white**: 15.0-16.0μm mean, σ < 1.2μm
- **Anything > 16.5μm** marketed as "premium" is suspect

**Cost**: $50-150 per sample. Most universities with textile engineering programs offer OFDA testing for under $100.

**Red flag**: A supplier who provides only "typical values" rather than your-batch-specific OFDA data.

## Test 2: Hand-combing visual inspection

Before any lab work, look at the raw combings. Real Albus goat fiber is:
- **Long** (36-42mm for premium, 32-38mm for standard)
- **Parallel-aligned** (herders comb in one direction)
- **Slightly bluish-tinted** (true white Mongolian has a natural cast, not pure bright white)
- **Has a soft hand feel** (low micron + good crimp)

Pure bright white fiber has usually been bleached, which damages the cuticle. If you run your fingers through a sample and get a "squeaky" or "plastic" feel, it's been chemically treated.

## Test 3: Dehaired yield check

Take 1 kg of greasy cashmere and send it to a processing facility for dehairing. The yield (dehaired output weight / raw input weight) reveals a lot:

- **35-42%** yield: high-quality Albus fiber, properly combed
- **25-35%** yield: standard Mongolian, possibly mixed grades
- **< 25%** yield: very short fiber or excessive guard hair (low quality)

If a supplier claims 50% yield, they're either chemically treating the fiber (which damages it) or blending with non-cashmere.

## Test 4: Color consistency within bale

A real "white" cashmere bale should have **subtle but visible color variation** within it — different goats, different body parts, slightly different ages all contribute. Perfectly uniform bright-white fiber is a sign of bleaching.

Take 5-10 random pinches from different parts of a bale. If they look like they came from identical sources, the bale has likely been processed (blended, sorted, or bleached) to remove natural variation.

## Test 5: Length distribution (Hauteur)

Use a **comb sorter** or send to a lab for **Almeter** testing. Length distribution reveals:

- **Hauteur (H) > 36mm**: premium, suitable for worsted spinning
- **H 32-36mm**: standard, suitable for woolen spinning
- **H < 32mm**: short fiber, only suitable for felted products or low-end blends

Short fiber shows up in finished yarn as pilling and weak spots — exactly what premium brands are trying to avoid.

## Test 6: Guard hair content (visual microscope)

Under 40x magnification, count guard hair fibers vs cashmere fibers in a 1g sample. Real dehaired cashmere should have **< 2% guard hair by count**. Anything above 5% suggests incomplete dehairing.

You don't need an expensive microscope — a $30 USB microscope with 40-100x magnification works fine. Count 100 fibers, classify each as cashmere (fine, crimped) or guard hair (thick, straight).

## Test 7: Supplier facility audit

The ultimate test: **visit the factory**. In one day at a vertically integrated cashmere facility, you can verify:

- **Herder contracts** on file (real direct sourcing)
- **Dehairing line** in operation (not just a trading company)
- **Bale tracking system** (every bale tagged from herder to customer)
- **OFDA equipment** in-house (means they test, not just claim)
- **Storage conditions** (climate-controlled, no direct sunlight)

A reputable supplier will arrange a 2-day facility visit including Ordos and a herder village. If a supplier makes excuses about visiting, walk away.

## Red flags that bypass any test

Even the best tests can be fooled if the supplier is determined. Watch for these behavioral red flags:

- **Refuses to provide per-bale OFDA data** ("We test but don't share results")
- **Asks for 100% upfront payment** before any samples
- **Refuses factory visit** or limits it to "office meetings" in Beijing
- **Sample quality doesn't match bulk order quality** (the classic "golden sample" scam)
- **Pricing significantly below market** ($60/kg for "premium white" is too good to be true)

## What to do if you suspect fraud

1. **Document everything**: emails, photos, video, OFDA data
2. **Test every shipment** — don't trust previous quality holds
3. **Build relationships with multiple suppliers** so you can switch quickly
4. **Use escrow or L/C at sight** for new suppliers under $50K
5. **Report to industry bodies** — The Cashmere and Camel Hair Manufacturers Institute (CCMI) maintains a supplier database

## The cost of verification vs. the cost of fraud

A 7-test verification protocol costs $300-500 per supplier. A single bad shipment of "premium white" that turns out to be 50/50 white/brown blend costs $5,000-20,000 in lost margin, plus customer trust.

**Verification is always cheaper than fraud.**

## Working with verified suppliers

If you want to skip the trial-and-error, we at DONGXIAO publish full per-bale OFDA data with every shipment. Our dehairing facility in Ordos is open to buyer audits, and we share herder contracts and bale tracking on request.

We also keep reference samples of every shipment for 2 years, so any quality dispute can be traced back to specific fibers.

---

### Private Label Cashmere Sweater Manufacturing: How to Build Your Own Brand from Ordos

*Published 2026-07-08*

Launching a private label cashmere brand requires the right factory partner, clear tech packs, and a realistic understanding of MOQ, lead time, and per-unit cost. A practical guide.

# Private Label Cashmere Sweater Manufacturing: Build Your Brand from Ordos

Private label cashmere is one of the few B2B product categories where the manufacturing quality directly determines brand perception. A good factory partner makes or breaks a private label business. This guide covers the practical realities of launching your own cashmere brand with an Ordos factory.

## The 3 private label business models

Before choosing a factory, decide on your business model:

### Model 1: Design-led boutique
- **Volume**: 300-1,000 units per style per year
- **Margin**: 70-85% retail markup
- **Capital needed**: $50-150K initial (inventory + sampling)
- **Target customer**: Mid-luxury fashion buyers ($200-600 sweaters)
- **Key success factor**: Unique design, distinctive brand voice

### Model 2: Commodity private label
- **Volume**: 2,000-10,000 units per style per year
- **Margin**: 40-60% retail markup
- **Capital needed**: $200-500K initial
- **Target customer**: Department store buyers ($100-300 sweaters)
- **Key success factor**: Price point, consistent quality, reliable supply

### Model 3: Bespoke / made-to-measure
- **Volume**: 50-300 units per year
- **Margin**: 80-95% retail markup
- **Capital needed**: $20-80K initial
- **Target customer**: Ultra-luxury clients ($800-3000 sweaters)
- **Key success factor**: Craftsmanship, customization, exclusivity

Each model requires a different factory partner and a different MOQ/lead time profile.

## 5 things to look for in a private label factory

Not every cashmere factory accepts private label work. The ones that do are usually **vertically integrated** (raw fiber → finished garment under one roof) and have an **in-house design team**.

1. **Vertical integration**: A factory that owns the dehairing line, spinning, and knitting can offer better pricing and tighter quality control than a "garment maker" that buys yarn externally.

2. **In-house design team**: Look for CAD pattern makers, sample hands, and graphic designers on staff. They can develop tech packs from your sketches, not just follow detailed instructions.

3. **Sample turnaround**: 7-10 days for counter-sample, 14-21 days for production-ready sample with your labels. Anything slower means they'll miss your retail season.

4. **Label customization**: Woven labels, printed labels, hangtags, and packaging sourced or made in-house. Many factories outsource this, adding cost and lead time.

5. **QC protocol**: 5-stage QC (incoming material, in-process, pre-finishing, post-finishing, pre-shipment). Ask for the actual checklist, not just a sales pitch.

## The 5-step private label process

Working with an Ordos factory, the typical private label process looks like:

### Step 1: Design brief and tech pack (week 1-2)

You provide:
- **Sketches or reference photos** (other brands' designs are fine as reference, never direct copies)
- **Yarn specification** (count, blend, micron)
- **Gauge** (knits per inch)
- **Size range** (S/M/L/XL or numeric)
- **Color palette** (Pantone codes or sample swatches)
- **Labels and packaging** (or factory sources these)

Factory delivers:
- **CAD pattern** (digital pattern file)
- **Yarn quote** (per kg by spec)
- **Production quote** (per garment by spec and quantity)

### Step 2: Counter-sample (week 3-4)

Factory knits a counter-sample in 7-10 days. The counter-sample uses the exact yarn and gauge you specified, in a standard size (usually M).

You review and provide feedback. Typical feedback rounds: 1-2 revisions before approval.

### Step 3: Production-ready sample (week 5-6)

Once the counter-sample is approved, factory produces a **production-ready sample** with:
- Your actual labels (woven, printed, or hangtag)
- Final sizing
- Final color
- Final finishing (wash, press, fold, pack)

This sample is what goes into your final production order. You typically keep 1-2 samples for your records.

### Step 4: Bulk production (week 7-12)

Lead time depends on quantity:
- **300-500 units**: 30-35 days
- **500-1,000 units**: 35-40 days
- **1,000-3,000 units**: 40-50 days
- **3,000+ units**: 50-60 days

Most factories split production into phases: 30% first batch for QC verification, 70% main batch.

### Step 5: Shipping and after-sales (week 12-14)

For your first 1-2 orders, **strongly recommend DDP shipping** (factory handles everything to your warehouse). This costs more but eliminates customs surprises.

After delivery, hold a **2-3% buffer stock** for quality issues. Most factories allow 30-day claims for manufacturing defects.

## MOQ and per-unit cost

Private label MOQ for cashmere knitwear:

| Style complexity | MOQ | Per-unit cost (USD) |
|---|---|---|
| Simple pullover, stock colors | 100 units | $35-55 |
| Standard cardigan, 3-4 colors | 150-200 units | $45-70 |
| Custom intarsia or jacquard | 300-500 units | $65-120 |
| Bespoke with custom design | 50-100 units | $80-180 |

**The "per-unit cost" decreases sharply with volume.** A 500-unit order of a standard pullover is around $42 per unit; the same order at 2,000 units drops to $32-35 per unit.

## The 4 hidden costs new brands miss

First-time private label buyers often underestimate:

1. **Label and packaging setup**: Woven labels are $50-200 setup + $0.10-0.30 per unit. Custom hangtags $30-100 setup. Polybags, tissue paper, gift boxes all add up.

2. **Sampling costs**: Counter-sample ($50-200), production-ready sample ($200-500), fit samples for size set ($200-400). Budget $500-1,000 for sampling before bulk production.

3. **Inventory carrying cost**: Cashmere knitwear is a fall/winter product. If you ship in August, you need 6 months of carrying cost (storage, insurance, capital tied up).

4. **Returns and defects**: Industry average is 5-8% return rate for private label cashmere. Budget for this in your margin calculation.

## 5 questions to ask before signing a private label contract

1. **"What's your minimum order quantity for private label?"** — Anything under 100 units is a red flag. Real private label factories start at 100-200 units per style.
2. **"Who owns the design after production?"** — You should own all tech packs, patterns, and design assets you paid for.
3. **"Can I use my own yarn?"** — Most factories allow this, but expect a 5-10% upcharge on production cost.
4. **"What's your defect rate over the last year?"** — Should be under 3%. Higher means quality control is weak.
5. **"Can you handle size runs and reorders?"** — Many factories offer "blanket PO" where you commit to total volume (e.g., 1,000 units) but call them in batches.

## Why Ordos is the right choice for private label

Ordos is the global hub for cashmere manufacturing:
- **38,000+ sqm** of vertically integrated facilities
- **500+ skilled workers** with 10+ years average experience
- **23+ years** serving global brands
- **1,200+ tons** annual dehaiiring capacity
- **ISO 9001, OEKO-TEX, GOTS** certified

For B2B buyers serious about private label cashmere, Ordos offers:
- Better pricing than Italian or Scottish cashmere (40-60% lower)
- Tighter lead times (35-45 days vs 60-90 days in Europe)
- Direct access to fiber sourcing (no middleman markup)
- Modern equipment (German STOLL, Italian dehaiiring lines)

The trade-off: longer shipping times to Western markets (25-35 days from China vs 5-10 from Europe), and a learning curve in Chinese factory communication.

### Small MOQ Cashmere Coat Manufacturing: How Boutique Brands Source from China

*Published 2026-07-08*

Most cashmere factories require 200-500 unit minimums. For boutique brands wanting 30-50 unit runs, here's how to make small-batch cashmere production work.

# Small MOQ Cashmere Coat Manufacturing: How Boutique Brands Source

Most Chinese cashmere factories quote **200-500 unit minimums**. Boutique brands selling 30-50 coats per season often assume small MOQ is impossible.

It's not. But it requires a different approach.

## Why factories set high MOQs

A typical cashmere coat production batch has fixed costs:
- **Pattern setup**: $300-500 per style
- **Yarn dyeing**: $800-1,200 minimum per color (even for 1 unit)
- **Sample knitting**: $200-400
- **Finishing setup**: $200-400

A factory's pricing assumes these fixed costs are spread over 200+ units. For 30 units, the per-unit cost jumps 30-50% to cover fixed costs.

Most factories prefer to pass on small orders. Not because they can't do them — but because the margin isn't worth the management overhead.

## 4 strategies for small MOQ cashmere production

### Strategy 1: Stock yarn + stock colors (lowest MOQ)

If you can work with **stock yarn counts in stock colors**, MOQ drops to 30-50 units per style. The factory uses yarn it already has on hand, so the fixed yarn-dyeing cost disappears.

**Trade-off**: Limited color choice (typically 3-5 stock colors per season). You have to design around the factory's stock.

### Strategy 2: Group orders with other small brands

Some cashmere factories offer **shared production runs** where multiple small brands combine orders to hit a factory's MOQ. You get the pricing of a 200-unit run while only committing 50-100 units yourself.

**How to find these**: Ask your factory directly. Some have standing programs; others will broker it if you ask.

### Strategy 3: Use the factory's own designs

If you're willing to white-label **the factory's stock designs** (with your brand label), MOQ drops to as low as 20-30 units. The factory has the patterns, samples, and yarn ready to go.

**Trade-off**: Limited differentiation. Anyone else white-labeling from the same factory has the same product.

### Strategy 4: Premium pricing strategy

If you can't meet MOQ, the alternative is **premium pricing** — pay 30-50% more per unit, and the factory will run smaller batches. This works if your retail price supports it.

**Math example**:
- Standard MOQ (200 units): $45/unit, retail $200, 78% margin
- Small MOQ (30 units): $62/unit, retail $300, 79% margin

The smaller batch still has comparable margin if you can position the product at a higher price point.

## The real cost of small MOQ cashmere

Let's compare per-unit costs for a women's cashmere coat:

| Order size | Per-unit cost | Total order |
|---|---|---|
| 30 units | $85-120 | $2,550-3,600 |
| 50 units | $70-95 | $3,500-4,750 |
| 100 units | $55-80 | $5,500-8,000 |
| 200 units | $45-65 | $9,000-13,000 |
| 500 units | $38-55 | $19,000-27,500 |

Small MOQ isn't cheap per unit, but the **total capital outlay** is much smaller. A boutique brand with $5K capital can do 50-80 units; with $20K they could do 300+.

## 4 things that work with small MOQ (and 3 that don't)

### Works:
1. **Stock yarn in stock colors** — factory's existing inventory
2. **Standard silhouettes** (crewneck, V-neck, simple cardigan) — no custom patterns
3. **Pre-made samples** with your labels — fastest, lowest cost
4. **3-4 styles per season** — not 10-15 styles; focus on what sells

### Doesn't work:
1. **Custom patterns for 30 units** — pattern setup is $300-500, hard to amortize
2. **Custom yarn counts** (anything outside 2/26 to 2/60 standard) — yarn mill MOQ is 500kg+
3. **Bespoke dye colors** — dyeing minimum is 5-10kg per color, hard to use up in 30 units

## How to make small MOQ work in practice

A practical path for a boutique brand starting with 30-50 units:

1. **Start with stock yarn + 2 stock colors** (cream, charcoal). Add a 3rd color (camel) in season 2.
2. **Choose 2-3 stock silhouettes** from the factory's design library. Customize only labels and tags.
3. **Negotiate** a per-unit cost of $60-80 with a 30-unit MOQ, and commit to a 12-month production schedule.
4. **Sample 5-7 pieces** before bulk production. Confirm quality and fit on real bodies.
5. **Plan inventory** carefully — small batch cashmere means sell-through matters.

The key mindset: **small MOQ is a financial decision, not a quality compromise**. With the right factory, a 30-unit run produces the same quality as a 200-unit run.

## Working with DONGXIAO on small MOQ

We accept small MOQ orders (30-50 units per style) for private label cashmere, with these terms:

- **MOQ**: 30 units per style, 50 units per color
- **Lead time**: 35-45 days (vs 30-35 for 200+ unit orders)
- **Per-unit cost**: $65-95 depending on style and complexity
- **Sampling**: $200-400 (refundable against bulk order)
- **Payment**: 50% deposit, 50% before shipment

For boutique brands growing to 200+ units per season, we offer **graduated pricing** — your first 30-unit run is at small-batch rates, but we lock in your pricing for future larger orders.

### Where to Buy Bulk Raw Mongolian Cashmere: A B2B Buyer's Guide to Sourcing Fiber, Pricing & Quality

*Published 2026-07-08*

Buying bulk raw Mongolian cashmere in 2026 means navigating origin fraud, micron variance, and pricing volatility. This guide covers where to source, what to ask suppliers, and how to verify quality before signing a PO.

# Where to Buy Bulk Raw Mongolian Cashmere: A B2B Buyer's Guide

Every cashmere sweater, scarf, or blanket in a luxury retailer's catalog started as raw fiber combed from a goat on the Mongolian plateau. The journey from goat to garment is long, but the first 200 meters — from the herder's comb to the spinner's hopper — is where quality is won or lost. This guide is for B2B buyers who need to source **bulk raw Mongolian cashmere** at industrial scale, with predictable quality and verifiable origin.

## Why "Mongolian" matters (and why it's not enough)

Cashmere goats are not a single breed. The premium fiber used in B2B wholesale comes from **Albus white goats** raised on the Mongolian plateau at 1,200-1,500m altitude. The combination of cold, dry winters, high UV, and specific vegetation produces the world's finest underdown — typically 14.5-15.5μm in diameter, with long fiber length (34-42mm) and high curl.

But "Mongolian" on a sales sheet is not a quality guarantee. The two largest scams in cashmere sourcing today:

1. **Origin laundering**: Fiber combed in Iran, Afghanistan, or Inner China (not Mongolia proper) is re-tagged and shipped as "Mongolian cashmere". The fiber is real cashmere — but the micron count, length, and color purity are noticeably lower.

2. **Grade mixing**: Premium white cashmere is blended with brown or purple fiber at processing. The bale ships as "white cashmere" but contains 20-30% lower-grade fiber that shows up in your finished product as pilling and color drift.

The fix is to source from a vertically integrated factory that **buys direct from herders under contract**, with full traceability from combed fiber to dehaired tops.

## The 4-tier cashmere quality ladder

| Grade | Origin | Micron (μm) | Fiber length | Price (USD/kg, dehaired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Premium white** | Albus goats, Ordos plateau | 14.5-15.5 | 36-42mm | $110-140 |
| **Standard white** | Mixed Albus / brown cross | 15.0-16.0 | 32-38mm | $90-115 |
| **Brown (qing)** | Albus goats, mature | 15.5-16.5 | 30-36mm | $80-105 |
| **Purple (zi)** | Older Albus goats | 16.0-17.5 | 28-34mm | $70-90 |

For luxury knitwear, you want **Premium white** only. For blending or mid-market products, **Standard white** is the workhorse. Brown and purple are typically used for heathered yarns or felted products — they dye unevenly in solid colors.

## 5 questions to ask any "Mongolian cashmere" supplier

Before sending an inquiry, vet the supplier with these five questions. Honest answers separate the real factories from the trading companies.

### 1. "Where exactly is your fiber combed and dehaired?"

Real answer: "Our dehairing facility is in Ordos Industrial Park, Inner Mongolia. We buy direct from ~200 contracted herders in the Albus, Hanggin, and Otog Banner regions within 300 km of our facility."

Red flag: "We source globally and blend for optimal quality" — this means origin is mixed and untraceable.

### 2. "Can I visit the dehairing facility?"

Real answer: "Yes, our facility is in Ordos Industrial Park. We host 50+ buyer audits per year."

Red flag: "Our processing partners handle that" — they don't own the production. Quality control is impossible.

### 3. "What is your typical dehaired yield from raw greasy cashmere?"

Real answer: "32-38% yield depending on grade. White cashmere yields highest, purple lowest. We track yield per bale to monitor herder consistency."

Red flag: "Around 45-50%" — that's chemically treated or blended fiber. Natural yield is 25-40%.

### 4. "Do you provide per-bale micron testing?"

Real answer: "Yes. Every bale ships with a Certificate of Analysis including laser-scan micron (mean + standard deviation), length distribution (Hauteur), and visual purity. We use OFDA 2000."

Red flag: "We test in aggregate" or "trust our quality" — no per-bale data means no quality control.

### 5. "What's your annual capacity and lead time?"

Real answer: "We dehair 1,200+ tons annually. Stock white cashmere: 7-10 day dispatch. Custom micron sorting: 20-25 days."

Red flag: "Unlimited" or "we source as needed" — no committed capacity means your reorder will be at the mercy of the spot market.

## What "dehaired" actually means (and why price jumps 2x)

Raw cashmere fiber combed from goats is called **greasy cashmere** — it contains guard hair (thick, straight, useless for spinning), lanolin, dirt, and vegetable matter. Before spinning, it must be **dehaired** — mechanically separating the fine underdown from guard hair.

The dehaired output is roughly **35% of the raw input** by weight. So 1 kg of dehaired white cashmere tops requires about 3 kg of raw greasy fiber. The price difference reflects:

- **Yield loss** (65% becomes waste or guard-hair by-product)
- **Italian dehaiirng line cost** (Capstan or similar, $5M+ investment)
- **Labor** for hand-sorting after mechanical dehaiiring
- **Testing** (OFDA micron + length per bale)

A "raw cashmere" quote at $30/kg is almost certainly greasy fiber; "dehaired cashmere" at $90-120/kg is the post-processing price.

## Direct vs. trading company: the 30-40% margin

Most B2B buyers in Europe and North America don't buy direct from a Chinese cashmere factory. They buy from a **trading company** in Hong Kong, Istanbul, or Milan. The trading company adds 30-40% margin and provides:

- Local language support (English, Italian, German)
- Smaller MOQ flexibility (factory MOQ is 100kg; trading company may start at 20kg)
- Inventory financing
- Logistics management

**For orders under 200kg per shipment**, a trading company is often the right choice. **For orders 500kg+** (the threshold where direct factory pricing makes sense), sourcing direct saves 30%+, but requires you to:

- Travel to China for an initial factory audit
- Pay 30% T/T deposit, 70% before shipment
- Accept 30-45 day production lead time
- Handle Chinese export documentation (or hire a freight forwarder)

## How to verify "Mongolian origin" claims

Three tests you can run on samples before placing a full order:

1. **Micron scan (OFDA 2000)**: Premium white Mongolian is 14.5-15.5μm. Anything above 16.0μm on a "premium white" sample is suspect.

2. **Color test**: True Mongolian white cashmere has a slight bluish tint (not pure white). Pure-bright-white fiber has usually been bleached, which damages the cuticle.

3. **Length distribution**: Premium Mongolian has 36-42mm fiber length. Below 32mm is shorter — likely from older goats or a different breed.

A reputable supplier will provide OFDA test data on request. If they refuse or only provide "typical values" rather than your-batch-specific data, walk away.

## Pricing trends 2024-2026

Raw Mongolian cashmere prices have stabilized after the 2020-2022 boom (when luxury demand pushed prices 40% higher). Current 2026 spot prices:

- **Greasy white cashmere**: $35-45/kg FOB Tianjin
- **Dehaired white cashmere**: $90-120/kg FOB Tianjin
- **Dehaired brown cashmere**: $75-95/kg FOB Tianjin

Pricing is largely driven by Australian merino wool prices (substitute for mid-tier knitwear) and Chinese domestic demand (which has been growing 8-12% per year since 2020).

For 2026-2027, expect prices to remain flat to +5% as Mongolian herding capacity is constrained by grassland degradation policies.

## Working with DONGXIAO

We are a **vertically integrated** Ordos cashmere factory: herder contracts → dehairing line → spinning → knitting. For B2B buyers seeking **bulk raw Mongolian cashmere**, our process is:

1. **Sample request**: We ship 100g samples of each grade within 5 days. Free for serious inquiries.
2. **Quality data**: Every sample ships with OFDA micron scan + length distribution + visual purity score.
3. **MOQ**: 100kg per grade/color. Mixed grade orders accepted.
4. **Lead time**: 7-10 days for stock grades; 20-25 days for custom micron sorting.
5. **Pricing**: We publish a quarterly price list. No hidden fees, FOB Tianjin or CIF your port.
6. **Payment**: 30% T/T deposit, 70% before shipment. L/C at sight for new customers over $20K.

For buyers new to sourcing from China, we recommend starting with a 200-500kg trial order before committing to a full-season volume.

### Wholesale Cashmere Shawl with Custom Logo: A B2B Guide to Woven Labels, Hangtags & MOQ

*Published 2026-07-08*

Custom logo on cashmere scarves and shawls requires the right label technology (woven vs printed vs embroidered) and proper hangtag integration. A B2B buyer's guide to private label accessories.

# Wholesale Cashmere Shawl with Custom Logo: B2B Guide

A cashmere shawl with your brand's logo is one of the highest-margin private label products you can sell. Retail prices of $150-500 per piece are common, and the production cost is reasonable.

The challenge: **getting the logo right**. Cashmere is a delicate fiber, and most logo techniques used on cotton or wool don't work on cashmere. This guide covers what works.

## 4 logo techniques for cashmere

### 1. **Woven labels** (most common)

A **woven label** is a small fabric tag (typically 1.5-2 inches wide, 0.5-1 inch tall) with your brand name and logo, sewn into the seam of the shawl.

**How it works**: Factory weaves the label separately (using your brand's logo and Pantone colors), then sews it into the shawl during finishing.

**Pros**:
- Looks premium (matches the cashmere quality)
- Durable (lasts the lifetime of the shawl)
- Doesn't damage the cashmere fiber

**Cons**:
- Setup cost $50-200 per design (loom programming)
- Per-unit cost $0.10-0.30
- 3-4 week lead time for label production

**Best for**: Brand labels, size labels, country-of-origin labels

### 2. **Printed labels**

A **printed label** is similar to a woven label but printed on satin or cotton tape, then sewn in.

**Pros**:
- Lower setup cost ($30-100)
- Faster production (1-2 weeks)
- Works well for small text and detailed logos

**Cons**:
- Less premium feel (printed vs woven)
- Can fade over years of washing
- Less crisp than woven for complex designs

**Best for**: Care labels, size labels, secondary branding

### 3. **Embroidered logos (direct)**

A **direct embroidery** puts your logo right on the cashmere fabric — typically in a corner of the shawl.

**Pros**:
- No label visible from the outside (cleaner aesthetic)
- Premium feel
- Long-lasting

**Cons**:
- **Can damage cashmere** if the backing is too stiff or stitching too dense
- More expensive ($1-3 per unit)
- Limited size (small logo only)

**Best for**: High-end brands with simple monogram logos

### 4. **Woven logo on the shawl itself** (most premium)

For ultra-luxury brands, the logo can be **woven directly into the shawl's pattern** during production.

**Pros**:
- No label at all
- Most premium look
- Logo won't peel or fade

**Cons**:
- **Very high setup cost** ($1,000-3,000 per design)
- 8-12 week lead time
- Only works for repeating patterns (not standalone logos)

**Best for**: Established luxury brands with 1,000+ unit annual volume

## Hangtag + packaging essentials

Beyond the label, a wholesale cashmere shawl needs:

### Hangtag
- **Standard size**: 2" x 3.5" (US) or 5cm x 9cm (EU)
- **Material**: 300-400gsm cardstock with soft-touch or matte lamination
- **Information**: brand name, country of origin, fiber content, care instructions
- **String**: cotton or natural fiber cord (not plastic)
- **Cost**: $0.15-0.40 per tag, setup $50-150

### Care label (required by law in most markets)
- Fiber content (e.g., "100% Cashmere")
- Country of origin (e.g., "Made in China")
- Care instructions (dry clean, hand wash, etc.)
- Size (if applicable)

### Outer packaging
- **Polybag**: clear LDPE, resealable zipper
- **Gift box**: 300-400gsm rigid box with ribbon (for premium SKUs)
- **Tissue paper**: acid-free, custom printed (optional)

For B2B wholesale, most buyers skip the gift box (retailers add their own packaging). But a custom polybag with your brand logo is table stakes.

## MOQ and lead time for custom logo

| Item | MOQ | Lead time |
|---|---|---|
| Woven label (new design) | 1,000 units | 3-4 weeks |
| Woven label (repeat) | 200 units | 1-2 weeks |
| Printed label (new design) | 500 units | 1-2 weeks |
| Hangtag (new design) | 500 units | 2-3 weeks |
| Custom polybag | 1,000 units | 2-3 weeks |
| Custom gift box | 500 units | 3-4 weeks |

For small MOQ orders (30-50 shawls), you can either:
1. **Use stock labels** from a third-party supplier (shorter lead time, but generic)
2. **Split MOQ costs** with another small brand
3. **Absorb setup cost** into your per-unit price

## How to brief a factory for custom logo

Send the factory:

1. **Logo file** in vector format (AI, EPS, or SVG). Raster (PNG, JPG) at 300+ DPI also works but less crisp.
2. **Pantone colors** for the logo (not just RGB or CMYK). If you don't have Pantone, give a physical sample.
3. **Label placement** — sewn at corner, center back, or hidden. Most shawls have a small label at one corner.
4. **Label size** — typically 1.5" x 0.75" (3.8cm x 1.9cm).
5. **Fold or cut** — woven labels are usually center-fold; printed labels are usually cut and sewn flat.

The factory will create a **digital mockup** within 3-5 days. Approve the mockup, then the factory produces a **physical sample** of the label within 2-3 weeks.

**Always approve a physical sample before bulk production.** A digital mockup looks great on screen but the woven fabric can look very different in person.

## 5 common mistakes to avoid

1. **Logo too small to read**: A logo under 1cm tall is invisible from a distance. Aim for 1.5-2cm.
2. **Using the wrong thread count**: Too few threads and the logo looks pixelated; too many and the label is stiff.
3. **Wrong label placement**: Labels in awkward positions (like the center of a shawl) hurt the product. Corners are standard.
4. **Mixing label types**: Using a woven brand label but a printed care label looks inconsistent. Match the aesthetic.
5. **Forgetting country-of-origin**: Most markets (US, EU) legally require country-of-origin on every imported textile. Missing this can result in customs seizure.

## Working with DONGXIAO on custom logo

We handle the full custom logo process for cashmere shawls and scarves:

- **Sample woven label**: 5-7 days, $80-150 (refundable against bulk order)
- **Bulk production**: 35-45 days including label manufacturing
- **MOQ**: 100 shawls per style with custom logo (lower MOQ for stock labels)

For new brands, we recommend a **3-step approval**:
1. **Digital mockup** of the label (3-5 days)
2. **Physical label sample** (2-3 weeks)
3. **Sample shawl with label sewn in** (1 week)

Total time: 4-5 weeks from logo file to approved sample shawl.

### Worsted vs Woolen Cashmere Yarn: Which to Choose for Your Product

*Published 2026-07-08*

Worsted and woolen cashmere yarns are spun differently and behave differently. Choose wrong and your finished product won't have the hand feel your customers expect.

# Worsted vs Woolen Cashmere Yarn: Which to Choose

"100% cashmere" tells you the fiber content. It doesn't tell you **how the yarn was spun** — and that determines whether your sweater feels smooth and drapey, or soft and lofty.

The two main spinning methods — **worsted** and **woolen** — produce yarns with fundamentally different properties. Choosing wrong is one of the most common mistakes B2B buyers make when sourcing cashmere.

## What "worsted" actually means

Worsted cashmere yarn is spun from **long, parallel-aligned fibers** using a combing process. The fibers are first carded (separated and randomized), then **combed** to remove short fibers and align the long ones parallel, then drawn and twisted tightly.

The result is a yarn that is:
- **Smooth** (long parallel fibers lay flat against each other)
- **Strong** (more fibers per cross-section = higher tensile strength)
- **Drapey** (less air between fibers = denser, more fluid fabric)
- **Less prone to pilling** (tightly twisted fibers don't migrate)

**Best for**: 12+ gauge machine knitting, suiting-weight woven fabrics, fine-gauge scarves, any application where smoothness and drape matter.

## What "woolen" actually means

Woolen cashmere yarn is spun from **random-oriented fibers** of varying lengths. The carding process randomizes fibers; there's no combing step. The yarn is then twisted loosely.

The result is a yarn that is:
- **Soft and lofty** (lots of air trapped between random fibers)
- **Warm** (still air is an excellent insulator)
- **Fuzzy halo** (fiber ends poke out, creating the "cashmere bloom" look)
- **More prone to pilling** (loose fibers migrate to surface)

**Best for**: 5-9 gauge hand knitting, chunky sweaters, scarves and shawls where softness is paramount, brushed or felted products.

## Side-by-side comparison

| Property | Worsted | Woolen |
|---|---|---|
| **Fiber length required** | 36-42mm | 30-36mm |
| **Yarn surface** | Smooth, clean | Fuzzy, hairy |
| **Drape** | High (fluid) | Low (structured) |
| **Pilling resistance** | High | Medium-low |
| **Warmth per gram** | Medium | High (trapped air) |
| **Gauge (knits per inch)** | 12-18 | 5-9 |
| **Cost** | +10-20% (combing step) | Baseline |
| **Best for** | Fine-gauge knitwear, woven | Hand-knit, chunky, brushed |

## How to tell worsted and woolen apart

Visual and tactile tests:

1. **Hold to the light**: Worsted yarn is semi-translucent (smooth, light passes through evenly). Woolen is opaque (fibers scatter light).

2. **Rub between fingers**: Worsted feels cool and slick. Woolen feels warm and soft.

3. **Untwist a 1cm section**: Worsted has parallel, smooth fibers. Woolen has random, jumbled fibers.

4. **Examine the cross-section**: Worsted is dense and round. Woolen is loose and irregular.

If a sample doesn't pass these tests, you may have a **semi-worsted** or **semi-woolen** yarn — which is fine, but should be labeled correctly.

## When to choose each

### Choose **worsted** for:
- **Fine-gauge sweaters** (12+ gauge) — smooth fabric, drapes well
- **Suiting and coating** woven fabric — fluid drape, no fuzz
- **Fine scarves and shawls** — elegant, smooth against skin
- **Premium blend yarns** (cashmere/silk, cashmere/wool) — adds strength
- **Anywhere pill resistance is critical** — luxury customers notice

### Choose **woolen** for:
- **Chunky hand-knit sweaters** (5-9 gauge) — soft, lofty, traditional look
- **Brushed scarves and stoles** — fuzzy halo is desirable
- **Felted products** — woolen structure felts more easily
- **Mid-market products** — woolen is cheaper (no combing)
- **Casual knitwear** — the "cozy" aesthetic

## Anti-pilling treatments

Pilling is the #1 quality complaint about cashmere knitwear. It happens when short fiber ends work their way to the surface and tangle.

**Two main strategies**:
1. **Use longer fibers** (Hauteur > 36mm) — worsted spinning naturally resists pilling
2. **Apply anti-pilling treatment** — enzyme wash that removes short surface fibers

Our anti-pilling treatment uses a mild cellulase enzyme that digests protruding fiber ends without damaging the yarn core. The result is a 60-70% reduction in pilling after 50 wear cycles, with no hand-feel change.

**Cost**: Anti-pilling adds $0.30-0.50 per kg of yarn. For luxury products where customers expect longevity, it's well worth it.

## Blending with wool or silk

100% cashmere is the most expensive option. For mid-market products, **blending** extends fiber and reduces cost without dramatic hand-feel change:

- **90/10 cashmere/wool**: 90% of the hand feel at 80% of the cost. Best for mid-market knitwear.
- **70/30 cashmere/wool**: Cheaper, but the wool becomes noticeable.
- **85/15 cashmere/silk**: Adds drape and slight sheen. Best for scarves and lightweight knits.
- **50/50 cashmere/wool**: Cheap, but loses most of the cashmere feel. Use for entry-level products only.

For blends, **worsted spinning** is essential — woolen spinning shows the difference between cashmere and wool fibers too clearly.

## Working with DONGXIAO on yarn selection

We spin both worsted and woolen cashmere yarn in our Ordos facility, in counts from 2/26 Nm to 2/60 Nm. Stock counts ship within 7 days; custom counts and Pantone dye colors take 15-25 days.

For new B2B buyers, we recommend a **trial run of 50-100kg** in your preferred spinning method and count, knit into a sample garment, and assess hand feel, drape, and pilling resistance over 4-6 weeks of wear.
